area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the accelerated stall, power-on and power-off, fly it from the right seat at 45 degrees of bank while you explain it, and teach it safely: set it up below VA and above 3,000 ft AGL, narrate it, and spot and fix the errors that turn it into a spin.
why: An accelerated stall comes at a higher airspeed and often a lower pitch attitude than the learner expects, it tends to be more aggressive, and without a quick recovery it can become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. It hides in badly flown turns, dive pull-outs, stall recoveries and overshot base to final turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. As a CFI you are the one who lets a learner feel it at a safe altitude before they meet it in the pattern [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]].

warmup: Think first: your commercial learner has flown good steep turns and good power-on and power-off stalls. Today you add the accelerated stall. In the first one they roll into 45 degrees, then yank the yoke back hard. The buffet comes 15 knots above the speed they expected, the nose is barely above the horizon, and the ball is a little out of center. What do you expect the airplane to do next, what do you say, and what would you change in the next briefing?

key_terms.def: Any stall that happens while the G load is above +1G, such as in a turn, a pull-up or another abrupt change of flightpath, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
The one AOA at which a given wing stalls, whatever the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Lift divided by the airplane's weight, in G. Stall speed rises with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The math is in AI.II.D and AI.IX.A.
The most speed at which the positive design load limit can be imposed by gusts or by full deflection of one control surface without structural damage [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A historical limit on certain airplanes: the most speed at which, at any weight, full control travel will not exceed the design limit load factor [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Reducing the AOA, and with it the load, by relaxing or releasing back pressure. At or below VA or VO the wing stalls and unloads before the design load limit is reached [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A turn where the rate of turn is too great for the bank, often from too much inside rudder [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A turn where the airplane is banked too much for its rate of turn and yawed toward the outside of the turn [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with little warning and roll toward inverted, usually the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A stall after a stall recovery, from hurrying the recovery before flying speed has returned [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
An aggravated stall with autorotation. It needs a stall plus yaw at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

chunks.title: Purpose, the entries and the CFI standard

body.p: The AFH gives three objectives for the accelerated stall: learn the airplane's stall characteristics, experience stalls at speeds above the +1G stall speed, and build an instinctive recovery at the onset of such a stall. Only commercial and flight instructor applicants may be asked to perform it on a practical test, but every pilot should know where it happens, how to recognize it and how to recover [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Frame it for your learner in one line: at the same weight, configuration, CG, power and conditions, an airplane at +1G stalls at the same indicated airspeed every time, but anything that puts more than 1 G on the wing (a turn, a pull-up, an abrupt flightpath change) moves the stall to a higher airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The AFH adds that the maneuver is typically demonstrated during steep turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. AC 61-67C adds that these stalls come from abrupt or excessive control use, are usually more severe, and are often unexpected [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].

callout.text: Do not reteach load factor here. Your learner should already own it from AI.II.D (load factor and the Vg diagram) and AI.IX.A (steep turns, VA and weight). Ask them for the 45 degree number before you start: about 1.41 G in a level turn [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: Purpose of and procedures for the setup. The AFH limits are short and absolute:

bullets: Bank: about 45 degrees [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Speed: never more than the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Flaps: never extended, because the design G limits are lower with flaps out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Number to know first: the published 45 degree, flaps-up stall speed, usually in the AFM [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: Two entries (K1). The common one starts from straight-and-level flight at or below VA or VO: roll into a coordinated, level 45 degree turn, then smoothly, firmly and progressively add back pressure until the stall. The other rolls into the 45 degree turn while still above VA or VO, waits for the speed to decay to VA or VO, and only then starts the progressive pull [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

callout.text: CFI ACS Appendix 3: for this Task the recovery occurs at the first indication of a stall (the evaluator does not ask for a full stall), and power must be set for an airspeed at or below VA. The skill elements S1 to S9 read word for word like Commercial CA.VII.D; the CFI applicant must also explain while flying and analyze and correct errors (AI.X.E.S10).
S3 says the evaluator specifies the configuration. The AFH rule against flaps still stands [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], so settle the configuration in the preflight briefing.

check.q: Name the three objectives the AFH gives for demonstrating an accelerated stall.
check.a: Learn the airplane's stall characteristics, experience stalls above the +1G stall speed, and build an instinctive recovery at the onset [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Aerodynamics: what changes in an accelerated stall

body.p: Start where every stall lesson starts: the wing stalls at one critical AOA, about 16 to 20 degrees depending on the design, whatever the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. The PHAK names three flight situations where it is most often exceeded: low speed, high speed and turning [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. The accelerated stall is the high speed and turning cases.

The dive pull-out shows the high-speed case best. The pilot pulls back sharply at 100 knots; momentum keeps the airplane on its old path for a moment, the relative wind does not change direction yet, and the AOA jumps from low to very high, so the wing stalls far above its normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Teach K2 as a table of what each factor does to this particular stall:

head: Factor
Effect in the accelerated stall
Source
rows: Angle of attack
The pull raises the AOA to critical while the airspeed is still well above the 1 G stall speed
Airspeed
More lift means more drag, so the speed may bleed off during the pull; holding altitude in a bank costs airspeed in proportion to the bank unless power is added
Load factor
Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor; the G pushes the pilot down in the seat
Power setting

The Task covers power-on and power-off. In the PHAK sample table (2,750 lb, gear and flaps up) the 45 degree stall is 64 knots power on and 77 power off. High power at high AOA adds a left yaw (P-factor) to correct
Weight
More weight needs more AOA for the same lift, so the stall speed rises; VA is lower at a lower weight
Center of gravity
Aft CG: less elevator force reaches the stall at a given load factor, and higher G is easier to pull in the recovery. Forward CG: the stalling AOA comes at a higher airspeed
Airplane attitude
The stall may come at a lower pitch attitude than the learner expects
Yaw effects
Coordinated, both wings stall nearly together; out of coordination, the bank may change until the AOA is reduced, and yaw at the stall is what starts a spin
Configuration
Flaps up, always, because of the lower design G limits with flaps out

callout.text: Application: ask the learner to predict, then fly, and then compare. 'Where will the buffet come today: above or below the POH 45 degree number, given we are 300 lb under gross with two people?' The answer is the weight row of this table.

check.q: In a dive pull-out, why does the AOA jump so much when the pilot pulls sharply?
check.a: Momentum keeps the airplane on its old flight path for a moment, so the relative wind stays the same while the wing rotates, and the AOA goes from low to very high [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

chunks.title: The entry speed limit: VA, VO and the speed you see

body.p: This is the part of the brief that keeps the airplane in one piece. At or below VA or VO, the airplane reaches the critical AOA, and the stall unloads the wing, before the design load limit is reached. Above VA or VO it can reach the design load limit at less than the critical AOA, so more pull can overstress it [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Intentional stalls practiced above VA can damage the structure [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

The PHAK's warning in numbers: when an airplane is stalled at a higher speed, the load factor equals the square of the speed ratio, so stalling at 1.7 times the normal stall speed puts on about 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Load factor is squared as the stalling speed doubles, which is why stalls at relatively high airspeeds can impose tremendous loads [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. VA itself and how it falls with weight are in AI.IX.A; use the POH figure for today's weight. The AFH puts the bank side of it simply: as the bank increases in level flight, the margin between the stalling speed and the maneuvering speed shrinks [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

bullets: VA protects one full input, once, in one axis, in smooth air, not several full inputs or inputs in more than one axis together [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Rapid, large alternating control inputs, especially with large pitch, roll or yaw changes, can cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]].

body.p: What the learner sees on the airspeed indicator. In the 45 degree turn the airspeed may decrease because the increased lift brings more drag [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. In the power-off version that decay is the normal picture. Application: in the power-on version the opposite can happen, so watch the roll-in and reduce power if the speed starts to climb toward VA (S4).

callout.text: Brief three numbers on the ground and have the learner say them back: VA (or the POH entry speed) for today's weight, the 45 degree flaps-up stall speed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], and VX or VY for the climb-out (S8).

check.q: Your learner rolls into the 45 degree bank 15 knots above VA and starts pulling at once. What is wrong, and what does the AFH alternate entry say to do?
check.a: Above VA the airplane can reach its design load limit before the critical AOA. Hold the turn, let the speed decay to VA or VO, and only then pull progressively [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Recognition: sharper, at a higher speed, and the limits of the warning

body.p: Stall characteristics as they relate to airplane design. Most trainers stall at the root first, helped by washout, so the ailerons keep some effect; but aileron used before the AOA is reduced can deepen the stall at the tip with the down aileron and roll the airplane further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A rectangular wing tends to stall root first with adequate warning; an elliptical wing gives little warning of a complete stall [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]]. The certification rule for small airplanes requires controllable stall characteristics and a clear stall warning in straight, turning and accelerated turning flight [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]].

What the learner should expect: in a level, coordinated turn the stall looks much like a wings-level stall, but the buffet can be sharper. If coordinated, the nose pitches away from the pilot because both wings stall nearly together; if not, the bank may change until the AOA is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Because the stall comes at a higher airspeed or a lower pitch attitude than expected, it can surprise an inexperienced pilot, and it may leave the airplane in an unexpected attitude [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

head: Cue
In the accelerated stall
Source
rows: Sight
The nose may be lower than in a 1 G stall, and attitude is never a foolproof cue
Sound
The air noise changes as speed falls; application: with the speed still high, expect less change than in a 1 G stall
Feel
The G load presses the pilot into the seat; seat pressure is how an experienced pilot judges load factor, and an accelerometer (G meter) can measure it
Buffet
Buffeting, uncontrollable pitching or vibration just before the stall
Stall horn
Devices alert as the critical AOA nears; many warn 4 to 8 knots before the stall
Full stall
An uncommanded nose-down pitch that cannot readily be stopped, perhaps with a roll. In this Task you recover before this

body.p: Range and limitations of stall warning indicators (R2):

bullets: The warning may be the airplane's own buffet, not a device; most vintage and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
AOA indicators are limited by calibration, unheated probes or vanes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].
With ice the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].
An autopilot can mask tactile cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102c]].

Application: the horn's 4 to 8 knots is a typical 1 G figure. In a firm pull the AOA climbs fast, so the time from horn to stall can be very short. Teach acting on the first cue (S6): the longer recognition takes, the more likely a full stall [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

check.q: How does a coordinated accelerated stall usually break, and what changes if the turn is not coordinated?
check.a: Like a wings-level stall but with a sharper buffet: the nose pitches away as both wings stall nearly together. Uncoordinated, the bank may change until the AOA is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: Where inadvertent accelerated stalls come from

body.p: Factors leading to an accelerated stall (K4, R1). The AFH says it most often happens inadvertently in improperly executed turns, stall and spin recoveries, pull-outs from steep dives and overshot base to final turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The PHAK adds that a sudden, unexpected loss of control in a steep turn or from an abrupt pull near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. AC 61-67C adds that the chance of an inadvertent stall from added load factor, as in a steep turn or spiral, is much greater than in normal cruise [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. And the AFH notes that stall accidents usually come from an inadvertent stall at low altitude, with the recovery not finished before ground contact [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

head: Situation
Why the AOA jumps
Prevention to teach
rows: Nose drops in a steep turn
Raising the nose without shallowing the bank tightens the turn and can lead to a diving spiral [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]
Application: shallow the bank first, then raise the nose
Pull-out from a dive or a recovery
Abrupt pull-ups at high diving speed can impose critical loads and produce recurrent stalls [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Dive only to cruise or maneuvering speed and pull up gradually once safely above the stall [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Late or rapid round out
Pulling back too rapidly to avoid touching down early loads the wing [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Go around whenever the landing is uncertain [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Turnback after an engine failure
Not lowering the nose enough in the gliding steep turn [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]
Practice at altitude, respond to any stall warning and reduce wing loading in the turn [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]
Base to final overshoot
Steeper bank, inside rudder and back pressure together [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; see the next section [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Stall practice entries
Pulling too fast on a power-on or power-off stall entry [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Raise the nose smoothly [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]

body.p: Stall warnings during normal operations (R3). A warning in a turn is the airplane telling you the wing is loaded. AC 61-67C says the response should be instinctive: add power, lower the nose and/or decrease the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. The AFH's turnback guidance says the same thing in a turn: respond to any stall warning and reduce wing loading [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. In the flare, by contrast, the landing attitude is close to the stall by design [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

callout.text: Knowing load factors and VA helps prevent two of the most serious accident types: stalls from steep turns or excessive maneuvering near the ground, and structural failure from loss of control in violent maneuvers [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

check.q: A horn sounds while your learner is in a 40 degree turn around a point at low altitude. What should they do first?
check.a: Unload: relax back pressure, shallow the bank and add power as needed; AC 61-67C lists adding power, lowering the nose and decreasing the bank [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

chunks.title: The base to final turn: the accident to teach

body.p: Make this the story your learner remembers. The AFH chain: an unrecognized tailwind on base gives a higher groundspeed; the pilot turns late or too shallow and overshoots the centerline; to fix it they steepen the bank, pull, and push inside (bottom) rudder to swing the nose around. The extra lift on the outside wing steepens the bank, the nose slices down, the natural reaction is more back pressure, and if it stalls with those inputs the airplane may rapidly spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Use the figure to show the trap. A skid is a rate of turn too great for the bank; a slip is too much bank for the rate of turn [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. Stalled in a slipping or skidding turn, the airplane can spin in the direction of the rudder, whatever wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. In the uncoordinated condition the airspeed indicator and altimeter can be unreliable, so the stall warning may be the first clue [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

bullets: Safest action for an overshoot: go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Low in the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees and never skid to correct [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Many stall/spin accidents have come from crossed-control base to final turns [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]], with the pilot trying to rudder the airplane around (skid) so as not to overshoot the runway or use a steep bank in the pattern [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

callout.text: Application: draw the pattern with a tailwind on base before the flight, then fly the accelerated stall and say, 'This is the same wing, at the same AOA, that stalls in that turn.' The demonstration-only cross-control stall (AI.X.F) is where you show the skid itself.

check.q: Why does inside rudder in an overshot base to final turn make the bank steepen?
check.a: The skid gives the outside wing more lift than the inside wing, so the bank increases and the nose drops through the horizon [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: Recovery: unload first, then a gentle pull

body.p: Fundamentals of stall recovery (K5). Reducing the AOA is the most important action in any impending or full stall; pilots who put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Follow the manufacturer's procedure when it is published and current (S7) [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

For the accelerated stall the AFH spells out the order: forward elevator pressure as required to reduce the AOA and eliminate the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, and adjust power as necessary [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. In a single-engine trainer without an autopilot or spoilers, four of the six template steps apply [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Do not try to fix the bank before the AOA is reduced; roll control improves a lot once the wings fly again [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

bullets: How much push: just enough. Every airplane needs a different amount, and too much puts a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Snapping the elevator forward can produce negative G that lifts the pilot from the seat [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
Power adds lift and cuts altitude loss, but it does not end the stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. As the speed builds, adjust power back toward the desired flight condition [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Trim: in a trainer most pilots can overpower the trim, but excessive nose-down trim may aggravate the condition, cause a loss of control or impose high structural loads [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
The pull-out: dive only to cruise or maneuvering speed and pull up gradually as soon as the speed is safely above the stall; that takes no more than about 2 to 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

The tradeoff to explain: a stall recovery trades altitude loss (and a gain in airspeed) against the load factor in the pull-up [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. A hard, early pull saves a little altitude, raises the G and invites a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].
Never let the airspeed or tachometer reach a red line in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Then configure as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY (S8), and return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator gave (S9).

callout.text: Relax, roll, power, gentle pull: AOA down, wings level with rudder, throttle as needed, then a smooth climb at VX or VY.

check.q: What load factor does the PHAK say a well-flown stall recovery needs, and how is it achieved?
check.a: No more than about 2 to 2.5 G, by diving only to cruise or maneuvering speed and pulling up gradually once safely above the stall speed [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

chunks.title: Secondary stalls, cross-control stalls and spins

body.p: The accelerated stall is the doorway to all three. Failing to recover at once from an accelerated stall may result in a spin or another departure from controlled flight [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Secondary stall: hurrying the recovery before flying speed returns [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. Because it comes in the pull-out, it is itself usually an accelerated stall, and the AFH lists stall and spin recoveries among the places accelerated stalls happen [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Fix: do the recovery again [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Cross-control stall: critical AOA with aileron one way and rudder the other. Little warning, a sudden bank change and possibly a roll toward inverted, usually the beginning of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Spin: a stall plus yaw at or beyond the stall. Yaw comes from rudder, adverse yaw from aileron, engine and propeller effects and wind shear [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Keeping the nose from yawing before the recovery starts is the key to averting it [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA while using too much or too little rudder, and to a lesser extent aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. In a skid the spin goes the way the controls are applied; in a slip with opposite aileron against rudder, it usually goes opposite the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. Spin recovery follows the POH [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]; it is taught in AI.X.I.

callout.text: Practicing full stalls can result in inadvertent spins [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The accelerated stall recovers at the first indication, but a learner who pulls hard and out of coordination can still get there. Altitude and hands near the controls are your mitigation [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

check.q: Why is a secondary stall after an accelerated stall recovery usually another accelerated stall?
check.a: It happens in the pull-out, when back pressure loads the wing above 1 G before flying speed has returned [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: Effect of environmental elements on accelerated stalls (R6). Each one adds its own load or takes away margin:

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a much higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. In extremely rough air slow to VA, but gusts can still exceed the load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Application: a gust during the pull adds to the pull, so the stall comes early and hard; choose smooth air for the first lessons.

Microbursts: a pilot who reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind shear is nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear hits, which can stall the airplane or land it short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Application: the reflex to haul back near the ground is exactly the abrupt pull this Task warns about.

High density altitude: altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, but true airspeed is higher for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]] and the engine makes less power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]. Expect a weaker climb after the recovery and more altitude used; spin altitude loss is also greater at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

callout.text: In moderate or severe turbulence, AC 61-67C says to cruise well above the indicated stall speed and below maneuvering speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. That band is the same one this Task trains.

check.q: On a hot, high afternoon, does the indicated airspeed of the accelerated stall change, and what does change?
check.a: Indicated stall speed stays about the same [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]; engine power drops [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], so the climb-out is weaker and more altitude is used.

body.p: Altitude (S2). The ACS wants the Task completed no lower than 3,000 ft AGL, twice the 1,500 ft AGL the AFH recommends for stall practice in single-engine airplanes [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Plan from the highest terrain in the area. Never teach stalls below a cloud layer that does not leave room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Collision hazards (R7). Clear at and below your altitude before the maneuver [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Raise the wing toward the turn and look in a high-wing airplane; lower it and look in a low-wing airplane [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. The airplane's attitude adds blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]]; application: in a 45 degree bank the raised wing hides the sky on the outside of the turn, so clear that side before you roll in. Haze and crowded practice areas make it worse [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The flight instructor should insist on a clearing procedure before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation (R8):

bullets: Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted from flying; intentional stall practice seldom caused one [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Task prioritization: budgeting time and prioritizing tasks leaves time to do them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Application: in this Task, bank and coordination come before talk.
Loss of situational awareness: failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC after a stall is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Disorientation: spatial disorientation is a lack of orientation about the airplane's position, attitude or movement [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. A sharp break from 45 degrees of bank can leave the nose low and banked; recover by the outside horizon cross-checked with the attitude indicator.

check.q: Your practice area's terrain tops out at 1,700 ft MSL. What is the lowest altitude at which the accelerated stall may be completed?
check.a: 4,700 ft MSL: 1,700 + 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.E.S2). Enter higher to allow for the altitude the recovery uses [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: On the checkride you fly and talk at the same time. Keep the demonstration in the same order as your explanation, and if it does not match, say so at once and explain why [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: 1. Brief: power-on or power-off, VA for today's weight, the 45 degree flaps-up stall speed, VX or VY, and the return targets [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] (S3, S9).
2. Clear the area at and below you, toward the turn first. Say: 'Clear right, clear left, nothing below' (S1) [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
3. Confirm the altitude gives 3,000 ft AGL at the bottom (S2). Flaps up [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] (S3).
4. Set power so the speed is at or below VA (S4). Say: 'At or below VA, so the wing will stall before it can be overloaded' [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
5. Roll into a coordinated, level 45 degree turn. Say: 'Ball centered, 45 degrees, holding altitude' (S5).
6. Increase back pressure smoothly and firmly. Say: 'Feel the seat pressure building and the speed bleeding off' [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] (S5).
7. At the first cue, call it: 'Buffet' or 'Horn' (S6).
8. Recover per the POH: forward pressure until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, power as needed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] (S7). Say each action as you do it.
9. Gentle pull-out, then configure as recommended and accelerate to VX or VY [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] (S8).
10. Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the evaluator gave (S9).

CFI ACS standard (AI.X.E)
rows: S2 Entry altitude
Task completed no lower than 3,000 feet AGL
S3 Configuration
As specified by the evaluator
S4 Power
Airspeed does not exceed VA or any other applicable POH/AFM limitation
S5 Turn
Coordinated turn in a 45° bank, increasing elevator back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall is reached
S6 Recognition

callout.text: Talking is what lets the bank wander. Glance at the attitude indicator as you finish each sentence; a bank that creeps past 45 degrees raises the load factor and the stall speed on its own [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

check.q: Which ACS element sets how far you take this stall, and how far is it?
check.a: S5 and S6 with Appendix 3: increase back pressure until an impending stall is reached, acknowledge the first cue and recover at the first indication (AI.X.E.S5, S6).

body.p: Ground first. Learners progress more slowly on stalls taught only in the air than when the types and the aerodynamics are discussed on the ground, and you should review the task before the flight even after ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For this Task the ground lesson is short: the 45 degree stall speed, VA, the entry, the recovery and the base to final story.

Building blocks. Teach it only after the learner flies good steep turns and good 1 G stalls, so the new idea is only the extra load. When several skills are taught together, simple to complex keeps a learner from getting frustrated [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Start power-off, flaps up, at a gentle rate of pull; then power-on; then both directions.

The anxious learner. Before the first one, review the aerodynamics, then describe the sensations to expect (the seat pressure, the sharper buffet, the nose dropping away) and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. If the learner reacts with fear, take the maneuver apart and demonstrate each stage, then let them practice the stages [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

Guard the controls. On hazardous maneuvers and especially on first attempts, be alert and ready to take control at any time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Anxious learners can be very strong; if you must, take over and calmly say 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: brief that a learner who keeps pulling after the break, or adds rudder against a dropping wing, is your cue to take over.

Letting errors run. Safety permitting, letting a learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out teaches more than taking over [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: a slightly slow pull or a late call can run; a skid, a bank past 50 degrees or a pull above VA cannot.

Realism. Tie the stall to the scenarios that cause it. AC 61-67C's engine failure in a climb followed by a gliding turn shows how much altitude a turnback costs, with emphasis on stall avoidance [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200c]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200c]]. Distractions while practicing are the most effective training method from the FAA stall study [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]].

callout.text: Check understanding by changing the maneuver: if the learner can only fly it to the left at one speed, they may not understand it. Ask them to vary it or combine it with another maneuver [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], for example a power-on version to the right.

check.q: Which two learner errors in this Task should you never let run 'to see what happens'?
check.a: Application: a skid at the stall, which can lead to a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and a pull above VA, which can overstress the airplane [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Safety permitting is the condition for letting errors run [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: Common errors related to this Task (K6). The AFH lists 18 errors for intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; the ones below are the ones that matter in an accelerated stall, plus the AFH's own limits for this maneuver. On the checkride the evaluator may make them on purpose for you to analyze and correct (S10).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area
Roll-in with no clearing turn or callout
Clear before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Entry above VA or VO
Airspeed above the briefed VA as the pull starts, often with power left in
Reduce power, wait for VA or VO, then pull [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]
Flaps extended
Flaps left down from earlier work
Flaps up before the entry [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]
Failure to maintain a constant bank in a turning stall
Bank creeping past 45 degrees during the pull
Hold the bank with aileron while adding back pressure [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Poor rudder coordination through the stall and recovery
Ball out of center; bank changes at the break
Coordinate with rudder; a coordinated stall breaks straight ahead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Inability to recognize an impending stall
No call at the buffet; the learner waits for the horn or the break
Name the cues on the ground and call them aloud [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Failure to act in time; full stall
The nose drops uncommanded or a wing rolls off
Recover at the first indication (Appendix 3) [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Level the wings or add power before reducing AOA
Aileron or throttle moves while back pressure stays in
Forward pressure first until the warning stops [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Not holding nose-down input until the warning stops
Forward pressure eased while the horn or buffet is still there
Hold the nose-down input until the warning is gone [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Failure to roll wings level after the AOA is reduced
Warning gone, but the bank stays in during the climb-out
Roll level with coordinated aileron and rudder once the warning stops [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Excessive forward pressure
Low or negative G, loose items float
Use only enough to stop the warning [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Inadvertent secondary stall
A second buffet in a hard pull-out
Let speed build, then pull up gradually [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Excessive airspeed buildup
Long dive, speed racing toward the red line
Start the gentle pull-up once safely above the stall [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and ball after recovery
Eyes stay inside; outside attitude and other cues ignored
Cross-check the outside horizon with the instruments [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Losing situational awareness
Wrong heading or altitude after the climb
Brief the return targets before the entry [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]

body.p: Application: one error is not in the AFH list but you will see it: a pull so gentle that the speed bleeds down to near the 1 G stall before the buffet, which makes it a slow-flight stall, not an accelerated one. The AFH words are 'smoothly, firmly, and progressively' [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Find the cause before giving the fix. A learner who thinks aloud shows you whether an error is a misunderstanding or a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner's recovery puts loose items in the air, then a hard pull brings a second buffet. Name both errors and the fixes.
check.a: Excessive forward pressure (use only enough to stop the warning) and an inadvertent secondary stall (let speed build and pull up gradually) [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

scenario.title: First accelerated stalls on a hot, bumpy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a CFI. Your commercial learner, 190 hours, is two weeks from the checkride and has never flown an accelerated stall. The airplane is a four-seat, fixed-gear trainer with a stall horn. With two aboard and half fuel it is about 350 lb under maximum gross weight. It is 31 degrees C at the 2,400 ft field. The practice area terrain rises to 2,900 ft MSL, cumulus bases are about 6,500 ft MSL, and there is light to moderate chop under the clouds.

questions.q: Can this lesson happen in the practice area today?
questions.a: Not as planned. The Task must finish no lower than 2,900 + 3,000 = 5,900 ft MSL (AI.X.E.S2), leaving only about 600 ft under the bases before any altitude used in the recovery. Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; find another area, change to a ground lesson or reschedule, all of which the AIH allows [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: You find a higher, clear area. Which VA do you brief, given the weight?
questions.a: VA is lower at a lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], so the max-gross VA is too fast today. Use the POH value for the actual weight (see AI.IX.A); the entry must not exceed VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] (AI.X.E.S4).

questions.q: In the chop the horn chirps during the roll-in, well before the pull. What do you tell the learner?
questions.a: A gust can suddenly raise the AOA and the airplane can stall at a much higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. The horn is real: ease the back pressure. Gusts add to the load of the pull, and in rough air the PHAK advises slowing to VA [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

questions.q: The learner notes the stall happened at the same indicated speed as at home, near sea level, but the climb-out was weak. Why?
questions.a: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], but the engine makes less power at a high density altitude [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], so the climb to VX or VY takes longer and uses more altitude.

questions.q: After two sharp breaks the learner is tense and asks to stop. What now?
questions.a: Stop for now and talk it through. The AIH suggests taking the procedure apart, demonstrating each stage, then letting the learner practice the stages to build confidence [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Before the next attempt, review the aerodynamics and describe the sensations to expect [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

questions.q: Rolling into a right turn, you see another trainer below on the right side. What now?
questions.a: Abandon the entry and keep the traffic in sight. Stalls lose altitude, so the area at and below you must be clear first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. The airplane's attitude creates blind spots, so look before rolling in [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15g]].

skills.do: Clear the area at and below your altitude, starting on the side the turn will hide, and explain why.
skills.practice: Do clearing turns with full callouts before every stall, raising or lowering the wing toward the turn [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed "no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)" and explain the choice.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write the area's highest terrain plus 3,000 ft plus your airplane's recovery altitude loss on the kneeboard.

skills.do: Establish the configuration specified by the evaluator, flaps up, and say why flaps stay up.
skills.practice: Say the AFH reason out loud each time: lower design G limits with flaps out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

skills.do: Set power so "the airspeed does not exceed the maneuvering speed (VA) or any other applicable Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH)/Airplane Flight Manual (AFM) limitation", explaining why VA protects the structure.
skills.practice: Fly both power-off and power-on entries and note where the speed settles in the 45 degree turn; adjust power so it never passes VA [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

skills.do: "Establish and maintain a coordinated turn in a 45° bank, increasing elevator back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall is reached", while you keep talking.
skills.practice: Practice the narration in both directions; have another CFI watch the ball and the bank while you speak [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

skills.do: Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn) out loud.
skills.practice: Call each cue by name as it appears: seat pressure, buffet, horn [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

skills.do: Execute a stall recovery in accordance with the POH/FM, explaining each step in order.
skills.practice: Read the POH stall recovery, compare it with the AFH template [[24:120|AFH 5-15]], and fly it until the order is automatic.

skills.do: Configure the airplane as recommended by the manufacturer and accelerate to VX or VY after a gentle pull-out.
skills.practice: Practice the pull-out at about the PHAK's 2 to 2.5 G or less, then the climb at VX or VY [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed specified by the evaluator.
skills.practice: Repeat the return targets back before each entry and fly back to them [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors when the evaluator, as a learner, makes them: name the error, say what you saw and give the fix.
skills.practice: Fly with another instructor who enters above VA, lets the bank creep or skids at the break; practice a one-line diagnosis and fix [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three AFH objectives for demonstrating an accelerated stall?
options: Determine the stall characteristics of the airplane
Experience stalls at speeds above the +1G stall speed
Measure the airplane's design limit load factor in flight
Develop the ability to recover instinctively at the onset of the stall
quiz.why: The AFH objectives are to determine the stall characteristics, experience stalls at speeds greater than the +1G stall speed, and develop an instinctive recovery at the onset [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Reaching the limit load is never a goal: at or below VA the wing stalls first [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: What does CFI ACS Appendix 3 say about this Task that a learner may not expect?
options: Power is set for VY, and the evaluator picks a full stall or an impending stall
Power for an airspeed at or below VA, and recovery at the first indication
Power is set to idle, and recovery waits until the nose drops on its own
Power is set for cruise, and recovery comes after 3 seconds of stall horn
quiz.why: CFI ACS Appendix 3: pilots must set power for airspeed at or below VA, and Task E is the stall Task where the recovery occurs at the first indication of a stall.

quiz.q: The PHAK sample stall table shows 77 knots at 45 degrees of bank. Which condition is that?
options: 2,750 lb, gear and flaps up, power off
2,750 lb, gear and flaps down, power off
2,750 lb, gear and flaps up, power on
2,750 lb, gear and flaps down, power on
quiz.why: Figure 11-34, gross weight 2,750 lb, 45 degrees: gear and flaps up 77 knots power off and 64 power on; gear and flaps down 68 power off and 56 power on [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

quiz.q: As the bank in a level turn steepens, what does the AFH say happens to the margin between the stall speed and the maneuvering speed?
options: It shrinks, because the stall speed rises toward VA
It stays the same, because both rise together
It grows, because VA rises with the load factor
It shrinks, because VA falls as the bank angle steepens
quiz.why: Stalling speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and as the bank angle increases in level flight the margin between stalling speed and maneuvering speed decreases [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. VA changes with weight, not bank [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

quiz.q: Besides the feel of seat pressure, what does the PHAK say can measure load factor?
options: The yellow arc on the airspeed indicator
The pitch of the stall warning horn
An accelerometer, often called a G meter
The slip-skid ball in the turn coordinator
quiz.why: Experienced pilots judge load factor from seat pressure, and load factor can also be measured by an accelerometer [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

quiz.q: Which rule requires controllable stall characteristics and a clear stall warning in accelerated turning flight?
options: 14 CFR 91.303, aerobatic flight
14 CFR 61.183, flight instructor eligibility requirements
14 CFR 91.307, parachutes and spin training
14 CFR 23.2150(a), stall characteristics and warning
quiz.why: 14 CFR 23.2150(a) requires controllable stall characteristics in straight, turning and accelerated turning flight with a clear and distinctive stall warning [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, how do stall accidents usually happen?
options: A failed stall warning device in cruise, with no other cue to warn the pilot
An intentional stall at altitude that turns into a spin the pilot cannot stop
An inadvertent stall at low altitude, with the recovery not finished before ground contact
A practice full stall that overstresses the airframe even though it is below VA
quiz.why: Stall accidents usually result from an inadvertent stall at a low altitude, with the recovery not completed prior to ground contact [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: Per AC 61-67C, why do pilots skid the airplane in base to final stall/spin accidents?
options: To slow the airplane quickly so it reaches the approach speed before the final
To turn the nose without overshooting or using a steep bank in the pattern
To keep the ball centered while P-factor yaws the nose at low airspeed
To raise the low wing when a gust rolls the airplane in the turn to final
quiz.why: Stall/spin accidents have occurred turning base to final because the pilot tried to rudder the airplane around (skid) so as not to overshoot the runway nor use excessive bank in the pattern [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

quiz.q: How much forward elevator pressure does AC 61-67C say a stall recovery needs?
options: Full forward stick every time, held until the nose is well below the horizon line
None at all, because adding full power alone always breaks the stall
It differs by airplane, and too much can hinder recovery with a negative load
Exactly enough to put the nose on the horizon, whatever the airplane
quiz.why: Every aircraft may require a different amount of forward pressure or relaxation of back pressure, and too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by imposing a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH ask of a flight instructor about clearing procedures?
options: Use clearing turns only before stalls and spins, since the other maneuvers stay level
Teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on it before all turns and training maneuvers
Do the clearing for the learner in early lessons so the learner can focus on flying
Let each learner invent a clearing method and check it only on the checkride
quiz.why: The flight instructor should teach the beginning learner an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use before all turns and training maneuvers [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

final_quiz.q: In the preflight briefing the evaluator asks how far you will take the accelerated stall when you teach it. Which answer matches the CFI ACS?
options: Recovery at the first indication of the stall, never to the full break
To the full break, since flight instructor applicants must show a full stall
Either one, as long as the learner calls the cue aloud
To the full break only above 4,000 ft AGL
final_quiz.why: CFI ACS Appendix 3 says the accelerated stall recovery occurs at the first indication, and S5 says to pull until an impending stall is reached. That matches the AFH aim of an instinctive recovery at the onset [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: A learner asks why stalls are so much more likely in a steep turn or a spiral than in cruise. Which answer fits AC 61-67C?
options: Load factor raises the stall speed, so the wing stalls at a much higher airspeed
A steep turn lowers the wing's critical AOA, so it stalls at a smaller angle than in cruise
In a steep turn the stall horn loses sensitivity, so its warning comes too late to act on
A spiral cuts engine power, so the airspeed decays all the way to the 1 G stall speed
final_quiz.why: The chance of stalling by increasing the load factor, as in a steep turn or spiral, is much greater than in cruise, because stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The critical AOA itself does not change [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: In the 45 degree turn the horn sounds at 82 knots, though the POH 1 G stall speed is 65. Your learner says the horn is broken. What do you explain?
options: The horn is set to sound 17 knots early in a turn so the pilot has time to react
The airspeed indicator over-reads in a coordinated turn because of the bank, so 82 knots is really nearer 65
The horn senses bank angle, so it sounds in any turn steeper than 30 degrees
The horn responds as the critical AOA nears, and the extra G raises the speed at which that AOA is reached
final_quiz.why: Stall warning devices alert as the critical AOA nears [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], and above +1G the airplane stalls at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator, as your learner, rolls into 45 degrees, then lets the bank creep to 52 degrees during the pull with the ball centered. Which AFH error do you name, and what does it do?
options: Poor rudder coordination through the stall; the bank will reverse suddenly at the break
Pulling too fast on the entry; the stall will come early, right at the 1 G stall speed
Failure to keep a constant bank; more bank adds load factor and raises the stall speed
Excessive forward pressure in the entry; the load factor will drop below 1 G
final_quiz.why: Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls is an AFH common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and in a constant-rate turn the stall speed rises as the bank increases [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The ball is centered, so coordination is not the problem.

final_quiz.q: Your learner says, 'Why not do these at cruise speed so I feel a real high-speed stall?' What is the best reply?
options: Cruise entries are fine if the learner pulls smoothly and stops at the horn
Above VA the airplane can reach its design load limit before the wing stalls
Cruise is fine in a utility category airplane but not a normal one
Cruise entries only make the buffet less noticeable
final_quiz.why: At speeds above VA or VO the airplane can reach its design load limit at less than the critical AOA, so more load can overstress it [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Intentional stalls above VA can damage the structure [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

final_quiz.q: In a retractable trainer the evaluator specifies gear down for the accelerated stall. What do the sources say?
options: The AFH bans gear down because gear-down G limits are lower, so you must decline the request
The ACS requires the landing configuration here, so the flaps must go down with the gear
The AFH rules out only flaps here, so set the gear as the evaluator and the POH say
The AFH requires gear down, so that the maneuver simulates the turn from base to final
final_quiz.why: The AFH forbids flaps because of the lower design G limits with flaps out and says nothing about gear for this maneuver [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; the configuration is as specified by the evaluator (AI.X.E.S3). Follow the POH limits.

final_quiz.q: Moderate chop covers the practice area and the learner wants to do accelerated stalls anyway. Which fact matters most for your decision?
options: Turbulence lowers the stall speed a little, so the stall will simply come later in the pull
Turbulence only matters in the traffic pattern
Chop affects only power-on accelerated stalls
A gust can suddenly raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a much higher airspeed
final_quiz.why: A vertical gust or wind shear can abruptly raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a significantly higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]; gusts can exceed load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

final_quiz.q: Recovering from a power-on accelerated stall, the nose is low, power is high and the airspeed is climbing fast. Your learner leaves the throttle in. What do you teach?
options: Adjust power as the speed builds; never let the airspeed or tachometer reach a red line
Pull up hard at once to stop the speed, whatever load factor that takes
Hold the dive until reaching VNE, then reduce power and start the pull
Keep full power on until the wings are level, since the power is what ends the stall itself
final_quiz.why: As airspeed increases, power is adjusted toward the desired flight condition, and the airspeed indicator or tachometer should never reach a red line in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Power does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and the pull-up should be gradual [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

final_quiz.q: You want to tie the accelerated stall to a real scenario. Which AC 61-67C exercise does that best?
options: Elevator trim stall in a go-around, adding full power with nose-up trim
Slow flight with the airspeed indicator covered, using various flap settings and distractions
Power-on departure stall straight ahead from VY
Engine failure in a climb followed by a gliding turn, stressing stall avoidance
final_quiz.why: The engine failure in a climb followed by a gliding turn shows the altitude lost turning back, with emphasis on stall avoidance [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200c]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200c]]. Not lowering the nose enough in that turn can cause an accelerated stall [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner keeps waiting for 'a real buffet' before calling the stall. Why is that a problem in this Task?
options: The longer recognition takes, the likelier a full stall, and this Task recovers at the first indication
It is fine, because the CFI ACS lets the evaluator ask for a full stall in this Task
It matters only in the power-on version, where the horn is harder to hear
It costs some altitude, but the stall itself will be gentler after the wait
final_quiz.why: The longer it takes to recognize an impending stall, the more likely a full stall will result [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. CFI ACS Appendix 3 says the accelerated stall recovery occurs at the first indication, and these stalls are usually more severe [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].

final_quiz.q: To lose less altitude, your learner pulls out hard the moment the warning stops. What tradeoff does AC 61-67C describe?
options: Recovery trades engine power against airspeed, so a hard pull keeps the power up
Recovery trades altitude loss and speed gain against the load factor in the pull-up
Recovery trades bank against pitch, so a hard pull levels the wings sooner
Recovery trades heading against altitude, so a hard pull holds the heading
final_quiz.why: Recoveries from stalls involve a tradeoff between loss of altitude (and an increase in airspeed) and an increase in load factor in the pull-up [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. Hurrying it before flying speed returns causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

final_quiz.q: During your demonstration the evaluator asks a question just as you start the pull. What is the best response?
options: Answer at length while you keep pulling, since the ACS wants you to explain while flying
Fly the pull and the recovery first, then answer; control comes before talk
Let go of the yoke and turn to the evaluator so the answer is clear
Ignore the question for the rest of the flight so you keep your focus
final_quiz.why: Prioritizing tasks leaves time to do them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]], and the AIH warns against teaching at an inappropriate time, when attention belongs on aircraft control [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: answer once the airplane is back under control.

final_quiz.q: Which set of AFH situations is where accelerated stalls most often happen inadvertently?
options: Long cross-country cruise legs, level-offs at cruise altitude and straight-in descents to the pattern
Taxi, run-up, takeoff roll and the first climb
Slow flight, power-off glides and normal approaches
Badly flown turns, stall and spin recoveries, dive pull-outs and overshot base to final turns
final_quiz.why: The accelerated stall most often happens inadvertently in improperly executed turns, stall and spin recoveries, pull-outs from steep dives and overshot base to final turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

takeaways: An accelerated stall is any stall above +1G: same critical AOA, higher airspeed.
Enter at or below VA or VO, at about 45 degrees of bank, flaps up, never faster.
It breaks sharper and can come at a lower nose attitude, so it surprises people.
Recover at the first cue: unload, level the wings with rudder, power, then a gentle pull-out.
Out of coordination it can change bank suddenly and become a spin.
Teach it as the base to final and turnback accident, after good steep turns and good 1 G stalls.
Finish no lower than 3,000 ft AGL, clear the side the bank hides, and guard the controls.
cfi_notes: Altitude: the CFI ACS (and the Commercial ACS) want this Task finished no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.E.S2), while the AFH recommends recovery no lower than 1,500 ft AGL for stalls in single-engine airplanes [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] and AC 61-67C uses 1,500 ft AGL for single-engine full stalls [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Teach the ACS number for this Task.

The AFH alternate entry says to start the pull 'at an airspeed 5 to 10 percent faster than the unaccelerated stall speed' after slowing to VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The same AFH page uses 'unaccelerated' for +1G flight [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], and PHAK Figure 5-54 uses 'unaccelerated stall speed' the same way [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Read that way it cannot be flown: a level 45 degree turn needs about 1.41 G, so its stall speed is about 19 percent above the 1 G figure (65 to 77 knots in the PHAK table [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]), and the wing stalls before the speed falls to 5 to 10 percent above 1 G. It may mean 5 to 10 percent above the 45 degree stall speed, but the text does not say so. Teach the common entry or the POH, and agree the entry with the evaluator.

The accelerated stall recovery wording differs slightly by source: the AFH says forward elevator, level the wings, coordinate, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; AC 61-67C (2000) says reduce AOA, then smoothly apply maximum allowable power [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Both put AOA first; teach the POH, then the AFH template.
The sources do not cover gear position for this Task; flaps are the only configuration item the AFH rules on [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Settle S3 in the briefing.
AI.II.D and AI.IX.A already carry the load factor math, the Vg diagram and VA with weight. Use them as prerequisites; this Task is about feel, entry discipline and the recovery.
PHAK's 1.7 times stall speed estimate of VA is only for older airplanes without a published VA and is a rough guide [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Always use the POH figure.
The horn margin of 4 to 8 knots is a typical 1 G figure [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]; no source gives the warning time in a firm pull. Measure it with your learner at altitude.
Learners often expect the nose to be high at the stall. Point out before the first one that the stall may come at a lower pitch attitude than expected [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
This Task is where the evaluator watches your hands as much as the airplane: model guarding the controls and calling the cue every time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
gaps: No source gives a typical altitude loss for an accelerated stall recovery in a light single. Measure your airplane's and add it to the 3,000 ft AGL floor.
The 45 degree flaps-up stall speed and VA for today's weight come from your POH/AFM; the PHAK table and the AFH are generic.
The sources do not say whether gear should be up or down in a retractable airplane for this Task; use the POH and agree it with the evaluator.
No source says how hard 'smoothly and firmly' is in numbers (rate of pull or G). Demonstrate it and have the learner copy it.
No source gives a teaching sequence for this Task beyond the general building-block advice; the order in this lesson (power-off, then power-on, both directions) is application.

activities.title: Numbers for the accelerated stall brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: AFH alternate entry, read literally. PHAK table airplane, gear and flaps up, power off: wings-level (1 G) stall 65 knots. What is the top of the band '5 to 10 percent faster than the unaccelerated stall speed'?
items.why: 65 x 1.10 = 71.5 knots (and 65 x 1.05 = 68.25). The same table gives 77 knots in a level 45 degree turn [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]], so in that turn the wing stalls before the speed falls to 71.5. That is why the literal reading of [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] cannot be flown (see cfi_notes).

items.q: Same airplane, 65 knot 1 G stall. Suppose today's VA from the POH is 105 knots (a given for this problem). In a level turn, about what bank angle raises the stall speed all the way to VA? Load factor = 1 / cos(bank); stall speed rises with the square root of load factor.
items.why: Load factor needed = (105 / 65) squared = 2.61. cos(bank) = 1 / 2.61 = 0.383, so bank = 67.5 degrees, about 67 [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At 45 degrees there is still a wide margin; it shrinks as the bank steepens [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

items.q: PHAK table, gear and flaps up, power off: 77 knots at 45 degrees and 92 knots at 60 degrees. During the pull your learner lets the bank go from 45 to 60 degrees. By how many knots does the stall speed rise?
items.why: 92 - 77 = 15 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Failure to keep a constant bank in a turning stall is an AFH common error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

activities.title: True or false: feeling the accelerated stall
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH says an accelerated stall is typically demonstrated during steep turns.
cards.why: True. An accelerated stall is typically demonstrated during steep turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

cards.s: Generous nose-down pitch trim is a safe way to speed up any stall recovery.
cards.why: False. Trim may be needed if the elevator alone does not respond, but excessive pitch trim may aggravate the condition or cause a loss of control or high structural loads [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

cards.s: The G load pushes the pilot down in the seat as back pressure increases.
cards.why: True. The extra lift raises the G load, which pushes the body down in the seat [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

cards.s: An airplane can enter a spin from a stall alone, with no yaw.
cards.why: False. An airplane needs to be stalled and yawed to enter a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

cards.s: AC 61-67C expects less altitude to be lost in a spin at a higher density altitude.
cards.why: False. Greater losses can be expected at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

cards.s: An accelerated stall may leave the airplane in an unexpected attitude.
cards.why: True. An accelerated stall may put the airplane in an unexpected attitude, and failure to recover at once may result in a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

activities.title: Teaching the first accelerated stall
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your commercial learner flies a 172-size trainer, two aboard, half fuel. The practice area terrain tops out at 1,200 ft MSL and there is some haze.

steps.s: The learner arrives late and asks to skip the ground brief and 'just fly the accelerated stalls'. What do you do?
options: Skip it; the learner already covered stalls in ground school
Fly it now and cover the brief in the debrief instead
Do a short ground brief anyway; stalls are learned better when discussed on the ground first
Brief it in the air during the climb to the practice area
steps.why: Progress on stalls taught only in flight is slower than when they are discussed on the ground, and the instructor should review a topic even after ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Teaching at an inappropriate time, such as during a busy climb, creates a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: At 5,500 ft MSL in the 45 degree turn, the learner yanks the yoke full aft in one motion and the break is sharp. After the recovery, what do you coach?
options: Pull even faster next time so the stall comes before the speed drops
Smooth, firm and progressive back pressure; abrupt inputs make it more severe
Hold the yoke still and let the speed decay to the 1 G stall
Use nose-up trim instead of the yoke to raise the nose
steps.why: The AFH entry is a smooth, firm and progressive increase in AOA [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; accelerated stalls from abrupt or excessive control use are usually more severe [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]]. Letting the speed decay to the 1 G stall is not an accelerated stall.

steps.s: Next one: at the buffet the learner calls 'Buffet!' but keeps the back pressure in to hold altitude. What do you say?
options: Fine; add full power and keep holding the back pressure
Add a little more back pressure to stop the sink
Roll the wings level first, then lower the nose
Forward pressure now: reduce the AOA first, altitude second
steps.why: Reducing the AOA is the most important action; pilots who put power and holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Do not try to fix the bank before the AOA is reduced [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: The haze thickens and two other trainers start working the same area. What now?
options: Stop maneuvering, find the traffic, and move to a clearer area or end the lesson
Descend under the haze to see the traffic better
Carry on; a clearing turn before each stall is enough
Turn on the landing light and keep practicing
steps.why: Crowded practice airspace and haze aggravate the collision hazard [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and an instructor can change the plan or end a lesson early [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Descending would also eat into the 3,000 ft AGL floor (AI.X.E.S2).
